exercises.title: I learn, you learn
texts:
When conjugating verbs, you remove "-en" from the infinitive form and add the appropriate ending. For example: The root of "lernen" is "lern-".
The first-person singular is "ich". Following "ich", the verb ends in "-e".
The second-person singular is "du". Following "du", the verb ends in "-st".

Ich lern#ps# Deutsch.
Du lern#ps# Deutsch.

exercises.title: Verb conjugation when using the formal "Sie"
texts: The formal personal pronoun in the second-person (both singular and plural) is "Sie". After "Sie", the verb always takes the ending "-en".

Matheus: Entschuldigung, wie #p# Sie?
Juliane: Juliane. Juliane Silberstein. Und wie #p# Sie?
Matheus: Wir heißen Santos. Das ist Adriana und ich bin Matheus. Woher #p# Sie?
Juliane: Aus Deutschland. Und woher #p# Sie, Herr und Frau Santos?
Matheus: Wir kommen aus Brasilien. Wo #p# Sie, Frau Silberstein?
Juliane: In Hamburg. Wo #p# Sie? Auch in Hamburg?
Matheus: Nein, wir wohnen in Rio de Janeiro.
Juliane: Was machen Sie hier?
Matheus: Wir sind Touristen!
Juliane: Ach so. Sie sprechen gut Deutsch!
Matheus: Danke.
Schreib in jede Lücke das richtige Verb.

pages.title: Conjugation: present tense (1)
texts:
In conjugation, the endings of the verbs often change. The ending depends on which person is doing the action. The ending comes after the verb stem.
Example: kommen
Woher kommst du, Nico? – Ich komme aus Spanien.
Woher kommen Sie, Herr González? – Ich komme aus Spanien.
Most verbs are conjugated in the present tense as follows:
kommen
Singular
1st person
ich komme
Singular
2nd person
du kommst
Singular and plural
formal address
Sie kommen
Example: heißen
When the verb stem ends in -s, -ß, -z or -x , the second-person singular form only adds a -t :
heißen
Singular
1st person
ich heiße
Singular
2nd person
du heißt
Singular and plural
formal address
Sie heißen
Example: sein
Ich bin Nico. Und wer bist du? – Ich bin Emma.
Ich bin Lisa Brunner. Und wer sind Sie? – Ich bin Sigi Körner.
The verb sein and other important German verbs are irregular. So always learn the verb forms as well!
sein
Singular
1st person
ich bin
Singular
2nd person
du bist
Singular and plural
formal address
Sie sind
Grammatical terms in German:
das Verb: Verbs are words that describe activities, occurrences or a situation, e.g. walk, eat, play. German verbs usually end with -en in the infinitive, e.g. kommen, heißen, lernen.
die Konjugation: When a verb is used in a different tense, or with a different person, it changes. It often gets a specific ending. This change in the verb form is known as conjugation.
das Präsens: The present is a verb tense. It is used when speaking about events, activities or situations that happen in the present or are continuing to happen.

pages.title: My name is Müller
texts:
Until the 12th century, people were only called by their first names. From then on, descriptive titles or "bynames" were given, like Heinrich the Great, or Anna the Industrious One. Family names, or surnames, became widespread from the 15th century.
Typical German surnames mainly stem from the Middle Ages, and are derived from artisanal trades. The most important occupations then are the most common family names now. The last name Müller (miller) is the most common, but there are also lots of Schneiders (tailor), Fischers (fisherman), Schusters (cobbler) and Webers (weaver). Some names have also been modified: Schmied (blacksmith) has become Schmidt; Bäcker (baker) has become Becker.
The family or last name is very important in formal communication in Germany. You address adults with "Frau Müller" or "Herr Schuster", as well as with the "Sie" form. Teachers must also address high school students 16 years and older with "Sie" if they are asked to.

pages.title: Name changes after marriage
texts: It used to be common for women to take their husband's name when they got married. This is no longer the case. Today, men can also take the names of their wives, or both can keep their own name. Married couples can also take double names; they keep their own last name and add on that of their partner. But for children, a decision has to be made: even if the couple has different names or double-barreled names, the children are only allowed to have one name.

lines: Lisa, Nico and Emma are about to drive on when Lisa runs into her friend
Max. Max asks Nico who he is and where he’s comes from. When it becomes
clear that Nico doesn’t know how to find his aunt, Max has an idea.
Hallo, Max, wie geht es dir?
Hallo, Nico. Du kommst nicht aus Deutschland, oder?
Woher kommst du? Ich bin Max und ich komme aus Deutschland.
Und ich bin Emma und ich komme auch aus Deutschland.
Ich bin Nico. Ich komme aus ... Spain?
Spanien, ja! Ich komme aus Spanien.
Wo wohnst du in Spanien? Wohnst du in Barcelona oder in Madrid?
Nico war auch am Flughafen. Er hat ein Problem: Seine Tasche ist weg.
Oh. Und was machst du jetzt?
Nicos Tante wohnt hier in Deutschland. Aber er hat die Adresse nicht.
Meine Tasche ist weg. Mein Telefon ist weg. Und die Nummer ist weg.
Und deine Familie? Kannst du deine Familie anrufen?
Kann dein Vater nicht helfen? Er ist doch bei der Polizei.
Mein Vater ist Polizist. Police. Vielleicht hilft er uns. Moment!
Ich komme aus Spanien. – I am from Spain.
